http://stackoverflow.com/questions/36404396/how-to-constrain-only-the-latent-intercept-in-lavaan

I want to constrain only the latent intercept using lavaan. I've tried the following:
fit_constrained_means <- growth(model, data=growth_data, group = "type", group.equal = c("means"), group.partial = c("i"))
However, when I compare this model to the unconstrained model, the difference in degrees of freedom is 2. Should it not be 1 since I am only (intending to) constrain a single parameter (i.e. the latent intercept)?
How can I make sure to only constrain the latent intercept?


Can you provide your full R script when you ask for help?  Judging from the model in your first link, it looks like you are trying to constrain a variable ("i") rather than a parameter (e.g., the mean of i "i~1" or the variance of i "i~~i").

The second mistake seems to be that you misinterpret the purpose of the group.partial argument, which is for naming exceptions (i.e., which specific parameters in the group.equal argument should not be constrained).  

Because you aren't constraining many parameters across groups, you might prefer to just use labels in the model syntax to explicitly constrain parameters that you want to constrain to equality, like you see in the answer to your first SO post.

Terry

messages.subject: Re: Stackoverflow and this mailing list
parts: What I am trying to achieve is to compare whether the latent variance differs across the two groups. How can I accomplish this?

Latent variance of what, intercept or slope (or both)?  As I suggested before, you can use labels to constrain parameters, as seen in the lavaan tutorial (look in the section "Constraining a single parameter to be equal across groups" halfway down the page).  After fitting a model without the constraints (mod1) and a model with the constraints (mod0, which is nested within mod1), you can test the null hypothesis that the constraints hold by using the anova() function:  anova(mod1, mod0)

Terry

parts: I just need to understand how to create the constrained model here.
From the tutorial page:
Constraining a single parameter to be equal across groups

If you want to constrain one or more parameters to be equal across groups, you need to give them the same label. For example, to constrain the factor loading of the indicator x3 to be equal across (two) groups, you can write:

HS.model <- '  visual =~ x1 + x2 + c(v3,v3)*x3
              textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
              speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9 '

Again, identical labels imply identical parameters, both within and across groups.


So, in your model:

model <- ' i =~ 1*t1 + 1*t2 + 1*t3 + 1*t4 + 1*t5 + 1*t6 + 1*t7 + 1*t8 + 1*t9 + 1*t10 + 1*t11 + 1*t12 + 1*t13+ 1*t14 + 1*t15 + 1*t16 + 1*t17 + 1*t18 + 1*t19 + 1*t20
s =~ 0*t1 + 1*t2 + 2*t3 + 3*t4 + 4*t5 + 5*t6 + 6*t7 + 7*t8 + 8*t9 + 9*t10 + 10*t11 + 11*t12 + 12*t13 + 13*t14 + 14*t15 + 15*t16 + 16*t17 + 17*t18 + 18*t19 + 19*t20
t8 ~~ 0.01*t8
t17 ~~ 0.01*t17
t18 ~~ 0.01*t18
# regressions
s ~ h_index
i ~ h_index

# constrain latent variance of the slope across groups
s ~~ c(vs1, vs1)*s'

Terry

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: Stackoverflow and this mailing list
parts: is it that you are using `s` that indicates that this is the latent variance of the slope?
I used "s" because you used "s".  That is the name of the variable in your model syntax that is the latent slope.  Its variance is defined using the usual lavaan syntax rules.
What if I wanted to constrain the latent slope parameter itself?

The latent slope is not a fixed parameter.  It is a variable, which has parameters that you can estimate or fix, such as a mean ('s ~ 1') and variance ('s ~~ s').  It is a variable because every case (row) has a different rate of change: the mean of "s" is the average of all the individual slopes.  If you want to force every case to have the same slope, you can fix the variance to zero ('s ~~ c(0, 0)*s'), which would make it a constant slope, implying it cannot covary with the latent intercept ('s ~~ c(0, 0)*i').
What that be `i`?

No, that is a different variable (the latent intercept).  You might want to search for some introductions to growth curve modeling to read (e.g., the first half of ALDA, with chapter 8 focusing on the SEM framework; or Preacher et al.'s booklet).
